content.text:
**Passport is the stronger award candidate. I’d enter it first, after one more editorial pass. I’d hold the website/wiki.** Passport gives me a question I understand, an action I can see, and a reason to take it. The wiki contains some of your most distinctive work, but a first-time visitor has to work too hard to find it.

**The best idea across both sites is “You finished your first song. Now what?”** It sounds like an artist talking. It leads naturally into rights, credits, and release preparation. And the campaign link carries that exact situation into Passport. I’d build the award entry around that moment. The black-and-gold art direction makes indii recognizable. The artist’s question makes it memorable. [See the homepage sequence](https://indii.music/#now-what) · [See the matching Passport](https://indii.music/passport?entry=first-song)

### Passport

**Keep the opening composition.** On desktop, the gold horizon draws the eye toward “Find my next steps.” At phone width, the orbital labels fall away and the primary button stays large, legible, and visible in the first screen. The first click goes straight into the assessment, shows progress as step one of five, and asks about the artist’s career. Including a returning artist and a producer stepping forward as an artist is a thoughtful detail. Those people can recognize themselves here. [Artist Passport](https://indii.music/passport)

I’d make two changes before submission.

1. **Make the royalty promise as precise as the assessment.** The introduction says “Find potential gaps.” A few inches later, the Royalty Radar card promises to “Uncover uncollected mechanicals.” The assessment uses the artist’s answers to recommend checks. An artist could reasonably read the card as a promise that indii will locate money owed to them. I’d use **“See which royalty registrations and split records to check next.”** That is a concrete outcome worth two minutes. [Artist Passport](https://indii.music/passport)
2. **Let the artist’s situation lead the campaign version.** On the first-song entry, “You finished your first song. Now what?” arrives in a small bordered panel, followed by the much larger generic question about business readiness. The more personal line deserves the headline position. Follow it with “In two minutes, see which credits, ownership details, and release steps to check first.” I’d also rewrite the first question’s supporting line, “We calibrate recommendations based on your operational complexity,” as **“Your answers help us suggest the right next step for this stage of your career.”** That would carry the homepage’s voice into the form. [First-song entry](https://indii.music/passport?entry=first-song)

### Website and wiki

| Priority | What I found | What I’d change |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Give mobile visitors a guide index** | At 390 × 844, the fixed navigation offered the audit, logo, login, and access. The desktop shortcuts to Release Lifecycle, Conductor, Pricing, and Founding Owner disappeared. After scrolling through the content, the page measured about **29,900 pixels**, roughly 35 phone screens. The desktop Pricing link worked when I tested it. | Add one compact **Guide** control with links to the existing sections. Send Passport’s “Explore Platform Guide & Wiki” link directly to that index. An artist looking for pricing or release preparation should be able to reach it in two taps. [Website](https://indii.music/) |
| **2. Put the artist’s problem earlier** | Before reaching “Now what?”, I encountered the independence headline, operating-system tagline, workspace explanation, Freedom Principle, Connected Intelligence, beta access, Studio captures, and waitlist. Several passages explain the same business proposition. The first-song and returning-artist examples communicate it faster. | Keep “Run your music career without giving it away.” Follow it with the situation selector and one piece of product evidence. Keep beta access visible in the header. Give the deeper platform explanation a home in the guide. [Homepage](https://indii.music/) |
| **3. Finish the presentation of the walkthroughs** | In Prepare Delivery, the video card says **“Real product clip planned”** and then invites me to play the capture. The deployed MP4 and English caption file both responded successfully. The public label makes an available asset look unfinished. | Replace the production note and “1080p HD • Synchronized VTT” with an artist-facing title such as **“Watch how a release package comes together.”** Put the duration next to Play. This is the smallest change I’d make before any judge sees it. [Release Lifecycle](https://indii.music/#capabilities) |

### The move I’d make for awards

**Follow one Detroit artist’s real release through both sites, with their permission.** Open with the finished song. Show one decision Passport helped the artist identify. Carry that decision into the exact wiki chapter that answers it. End on something the artist actually made or completed, such as a finished credit sheet or delivery-ready release package. A short listening excerpt, the artist’s own words, and one well-captioned product capture would give the gold visual system a human subject.

That story would also give you a clear editorial test. Every effect, headline, and interaction should help the visitor understand what happened to this artist and what they could do for their own music. I’d spend the next design pass on that story and mobile wayfinding. Awwwards’ published mobile guidance explicitly evaluates discoverability, legibility, visible primary actions, and touch targets. [Awwwards mobile evaluation guidelines](https://www.awwwards.com/mobile-excellence-guidelines.pdf)

**Review scope.** I reviewed the public production sites signed out in Chrome at desktop and phone viewport sizes, opened the first assessment step, checked the campaign-specific Passport, followed the Passport-to-website handoff, and tested section navigation. Account creation, plan assignment, completed assessment results, email delivery, and physical-device performance remain unverified.

All right, so I just wanna comment real quick on the only thing that I've read so far which is the move I'd make for awards, I could give you a high five if you if you had a hand because I'm literally literally working on that right now relative to you know reading what you said otherwise but I have somebody. I'm waiting to hear from that Detroit techno artist they're out of town until Frid, which is today so maybe I'll hear from him this weekend but soon this person is somebody that actually has been following my Instagram so it kinda could work out real good so what that said let's try to let's try to put that plan together and what what it would look like high-level and then we'll work on bringing it closer as we get this person in line.

I’d build it around **one Detroit techno track and one real decision its artist has to make.** The artist already follows you on Instagram, so when you hear back, you can start with the music and see what they’d genuinely want to share. The story will come from what’s happening with their release.

## The experience

| Moment | What the visitor sees |
|---|---|
| **Hear the track** | Open on the artist in their own words, with a short, opt-in listening excerpt. Give them one line to explain where the track is in its life and what’s on their mind. |
| **“Now what?”** | Put their actual question on screen. Maybe it’s how to credit a collaborator, prepare a release package, or organize a record that’s already out. Their situation determines the story. |
| **Follow the decision** | Show the moment in Passport that helped surface a next step, then take visitors straight to the relevant wiki chapter. One short product capture can show the artist working through it. |
| **See what came out of it** | End with something the artist actually finished or decided. A credit sheet, a release checklist, or an approved package would each give the story a tangible payoff. Close with the artist’s own words and **“Find my next steps.”** |

On the **website**, this could be the featured “Now what?” story, with the track, the artist, and the full walkthrough. On **Passport**, it can be a short invitation into the assessment. Someone arriving from Instagram should recognize the same track and question immediately and be able to start in one tap.

## Before and after you hear back

**Now**, we can settle the shape of the piece. I’d plan for one featured story, one short product capture, and one matching Passport entry. Keep the track, the central question, and the outcome open. That gives us enough structure to move quickly once we know what the artist is working on.

**Once they’re interested**, start with a short conversation before planning a shoot. I’d ask:

- “Is there a track you’re working on or putting out that you’d be comfortable talking about?”
- “What’s the next decision you’re trying to make with it?”
- “What parts of that process would you enjoy showing?”

From there, pick a step they genuinely want to take, capture it as it happens, and have them approve the story and where their music, name, and image can appear, including any award materials.

The first milestone is simple. **Come out of that conversation with a track and a question the artist cares about.** Once we have those, we can write the opening, choose the exact guide chapter, and build the shot list around what’s real.

Okay, so your recommendations are all good. If you have questions, I'm here to answer them real quick so we can move forward. I am waiting on an artist already to get back with me to do exactly what you were saying what you would do, which is, you know, get a local artist to run some tracks through here. One caveat is I don't necessarily have the fees paid that I need to, particularly to release music. But we'll get to that

We can start with **one Detroit artist and one real track, with release preparation as the first milestone.** That gives us a complete story even while the release fees are pending. If the artist brings several tracks, I’d let them choose one to feature and keep the others private.

Here’s how I’d run the pilot:

1. **Pick the track and the decision.** Start with “What are you trying to do next with this record?” Let the artist’s answer guide the session. They might need to confirm a collaborator’s credit, pull together release materials, or figure out what’s missing before delivery.
2. **Run the track through Passport and take one useful step.** Follow the recommendation into the relevant wiki section, then work through that step together. Capture what the artist came in with, what they decided, and what they left with. A completed credits sheet or a release checklist with clear next actions can be the payoff.
3. **Build the public story from that session.** The website gets the artist’s question, a short listening excerpt if they approve it, and the walkthrough. Passport gets the same question as an invitation for visitors to find their own next step. Let the artist review the excerpt, footage, and wording before anything goes public or into an award submission.

When the artist gets back to you, I’d open with **“Got a track you’d like to move forward? Let’s spend half an hour on whatever’s next for it and see what we can get done.”** A half hour is a starting point for the first session. Once you know the track and the sticking point, we can build the specific walkthrough around them. If the record goes live later, that gives the story a second chapter.
So make the changes to the copy that you are recommending
I’ll update the Passport promises and campaign headlines, simplify the first assessment prompt, and clean up the walkthrough copy on the website.
